title: Soil Mechanics
description: Practice questions covering compaction, consolidation, deep & shallow foundations, earth pressure, index properties, permeability, seepage, shear strength, soil classification, soil exploration, and slope stability — organized by chapter in original document order.

questions.text: The advantage of compaction of soil are:
questions.expl: Compaction densifies soil, which improves shear strength, cuts down future settlement, and reduces swelling potential — so all three benefits apply together.

questions.text: For an Indian standard compaction test the mass of hammer and the drop of hammer are:
questions.expl: IS light (Proctor) compaction uses a 2.6 kg rammer falling through 310 mm, compacted in 3 layers of 25 blows each in a 1000 cc mould.

questions.text: Vibratory rollers are best suited for compacting:
questions.expl: Vibratory compaction works by rearranging cohesionless grains through vibration, making it ideal for coarse sands and gravels rather than plastic clays.

questions.text: Standard proctor test is used for determining
questions.expl: The standard Proctor test plots dry density against water content to find the optimum moisture content (OMC) that gives maximum dry density.

questions.text: For cohesive soils, with increasing compactive effort, the optimum moisture content
questions.expl: As compactive effort rises, less water is needed to reach maximum dry density, so OMC decreases for cohesive soils.

questions.text: In compaction test, MDD stands for maximum dry density and OMC for optimum moisture content. As compaction energy increases,
options: No change in MDD and OMC
questions.expl: Higher compaction energy pushes particles closer together at lower water content, so MDD increases while OMC decreases.

questions.text: Coarse grained soils are best compacted by a
questions.expl: Vibratory rollers transmit vibrations that rearrange cohesionless coarse particles efficiently, making them best for coarse-grained soils.

questions.text: For better strength and stability, the fine grained soils and coarse grained soils are compacted respectively as (where OMC is optimum moisture content)
options: Dry of OMC and wet of OMC
Wet of OMC and dry of OMC
Wet of OMC and wet of OMC
Dry of OMC and dry of OMC
questions.expl: Fine-grained (cohesive) soils are compacted wet of OMC for a dispersed, ductile structure giving better strength/stability, while coarse-grained soils are compacted wet of OMC too for particle rearrangement — per Lambe's classic guidance the standard answer is wet of OMC for fines and dry of OMC for coarse, matching option B.

questions.text: Sheep foot rollers are recommended for compacting
questions.expl: The feet of a sheep foot roller knead and remould the soil, so it works best on cohesive (clayey) soils.

questions.text: Relative compaction of the soil is
questions.expl: Relative compaction is the ratio of field dry density to laboratory maximum dry density, expressed as a percentage.

questions.text: Optimum moisture content is moisture content at which
questions.expl: OMC is defined as the water content at which the soil reaches its maximum dry density for a given compactive effort.

questions.text: In a compaction test in which the compacting effort increases, the optimum moisture content
questions.expl: Greater compacting effort needs less water to reach maximum density, so OMC decreases.

questions.text: Compaction of a soil is measured in terms of
questions.expl: Dry density (mass of solids per unit total volume) is the standard measure used to judge compaction quality.

questions.text: Compaction of soil is aimed at
questions.expl: Compaction packs particles closer together, expelling air, which decreases the void ratio.

questions.text: The process of compaction of a soil involves
options: Expulsion of both pore water and air voids
questions.expl: Compaction mainly expels air from the voids; pore water is not readily expelled at typical compaction water contents (that's consolidation instead), so option B is correct.

questions.text: Compaction of a soil
questions.expl: Since compaction reduces void ratio it simultaneously increases dry density and decreases porosity — both A and B occur together.

questions.text: The most effective method for compacting sand is by using
questions.expl: For cohesionless sand, vibration rearranges grains far more effectively than rolling or kneading, so vibratory methods work best.

questions.text: The soil involved in the compaction is
questions.expl: Compaction is generally carried out on partly saturated soil, where air voids can still be expelled by mechanical effort.

questions.text: The maximum dry density up to which any soil can be compacted depends upon
options: Both water content and compactive effort
questions.expl: The maximum dry density achievable depends on both the water content used and the amount of compactive energy applied.

questions.text: Compaction process may be accompanied by
questions.expl: Field compaction can be achieved by rolling, tamping, or vibration — any of these mechanical means is valid.

questions.text: The maximum compaction for any given water content corresponds to a percent air voids equal to
questions.expl: The theoretical maximum (zero air voids) line corresponds to 0% air voids, representing full saturation at that density.

questions.text: In the modified proctor test the drop height of the rammer is
questions.expl: The modified Proctor test uses a heavier rammer with a greater drop height of 45 cm (450 mm) compared to the standard test's 310 mm.

questions.text: Degree of consolidation depends upon
questions.expl: Degree of consolidation depends on the thickness of the clay layer, its permeability, and its coefficient of consolidation — i.e., all of these.

questions.text: Match List I with List II: A. Sheep foot roller, B. Smooth heavy roller, C. Pneumatic roller, D. Vibration roller with 1. Hearting of earthen dam, 2. Dry sand, 3. Casting of earthen dam, 4. Gravel in WBM road. Codes:
questions.expl: Sheep foot rollers work the impervious hearting core of a dam; smooth rollers compact dry, cohesionless sand; pneumatic rollers are used for general casting/facing of earthen dams; vibratory rollers compact gravel in WBM roads, giving the pairing A-3, B-2, C-1... matching the listed code (b).

questions.text: Plasticity needle is used to determine
options: Penetration resistance to control field compaction
Penetration value of bitumen used in road construction
Swelling index of black cotton soils
questions.expl: The plasticity needle (Proctor penetration needle) measures penetration resistance, which is used to control field compaction moisture content.

questions.text: The number of blows required for compaction of each layer of soil in the compaction test is
questions.expl: The IS light compaction test uses 25 blows per layer for 3 layers in a 1000 cc mould.

questions.text: Factors affecting the compaction is/are
questions.expl: Compaction outcome depends jointly on water content, compactive energy applied, and the type of soil being compacted.

questions.text: The 95% saturation line and 5% air voids line are
questions.expl: At a given dry density, the 5% air-voids line and the 95% saturation line represent essentially the same locus, since 5% air voids corresponds to 95% degree of saturation.

questions.text: Consolidation theory was enunciated by
questions.expl: The one-dimensional theory of consolidation was developed by Karl Terzaghi.

questions.text: Rate of consolidation of soil
options: Is unaffected by permeability of soil
questions.expl: Higher temperature lowers the viscosity of pore water, allowing it to escape faster, so the rate of consolidation increases with temperature.

questions.text: Root time method is used to determine
questions.expl: The square-root-of-time (Taylor's) fitting method is used to determine the coefficient of consolidation, Cv.

questions.text: Consolidation time of a soil sample:
options: Increases with an increase in permeability
Increases with a decreases in permeability
Increases with a decreases in compressibility
questions.expl: Lower permeability slows the escape of pore water, so consolidation takes longer as permeability decreases.

questions.text: The degree of consolidation is directly proportional
options: To drainage path and inversely to time
To time and inversely to drainage path
To time and inversely to the square of drainage path
questions.expl: Degree of consolidation U is a function of time factor Tv, which is directly proportional to time and inversely proportional to the square of the drainage path.

questions.text: Elastic settlement of a shallow foundation clayey soil occurs due to
options: Rapid release of excess pore pressure
Breakage of primary structure of soil
questions.expl: Elastic (immediate) settlement in clay arises from shear distortion of the soil skeleton under load, without volume change.

questions.text: The ratio of settlement at any time 't' to the final settlement is known as
questions.expl: The degree of consolidation is precisely defined as settlement at time t divided by the final (ultimate) settlement.

questions.text: For routine consolidation test in laboratory, the thickness of the specimen is
questions.expl: A standard consolidation (oedometer) test specimen is typically about 20 mm thick.

questions.text: The consolidation time for soils
options: Is independent of the stress change
questions.expl: Consolidation time increases with compressibility, decreases with permeability, and depends on the applied stress increment — so it depends on multiple factors together.

questions.text: Compressibility of sandy soils is
options: Almost equal to that of clayey soils
Much greater than that of clayey soils
Much less than that of clayey soils
questions.expl: Sands are far stiffer and less compressible than clays, so their compressibility is much less than that of clayey soils.

questions.text: Time factor for a clay layer is
options: Inversely proportional to permeability of soil
Inversely proportional to square of drainage path
Independent of thickness of clay layer
questions.expl: Time factor Tv = Cv t / d^2, so it is inversely proportional to the square of the drainage path length.

questions.text: In consolidation testing, curve fitting method is used to determine
questions.expl: The curve fitting (square-root-of-time or log-time) method is a standard technique for determining the coefficient of consolidation Cv from lab data.

questions.text: The natural void ratio of a saturated clay strata, 3 m thick, is 0.90. The final void ratio of the clay at the end of consolidation is expected to be 0.71. The total consolidation settlement of the clay strata is

A saturated clay layer with double drainage takes 5 years to attain 90% degree of consolidation under a structure. If the same layer were to be single drained, what would be the time (in years) required to attain the same consolidation under the same loading conditions?
questions.expl: Halving the drainage path (single vs double drainage) quadruples the time for the same degree of consolidation, since t is proportional to d^2: 5 x 4 = 20 years.

questions.text: A clay layer 5 m thick in field takes 300 days to attain 50% consolidation with condition of double drainage. If the same clay layer is underlain by hard rock then the time taken to attain 50% consolidation will be
questions.expl: With single drainage the path doubles, so time for the same consolidation quadruples: 300 x 4 = 1200 days.

questions.text: A clayey sample of 2 cm thickness is collected from a 30 cm thick clayey strata resting on impermeable rock. In a consolidation test, this clayey sample took time t1 to achieve 30% consolidation. If t2 is the time required to achieve 50% consolidation for the soil sample then the ratio t2/t1 will be
questions.expl: Since Tv is proportional to t/d^2, and the two cases share the same soil, t2/t1 is found from the ratio of time factors for U=50% and U=30%, giving about 2.78.

questions.text: Rate of settlement of a compressible layer is dependent upon
options: Applied load, thickness of layer and time factor
Thickness of layer and time factor
Applied load and thickness of layer
questions.expl: Settlement rate depends on the applied load (which drives excess pore pressure), the thickness of the compressible layer, and the time factor governing dissipation.

questions.text: Reduction in volume of soil primarily due to squeezing out of water from the voids is called
questions.expl: Squeezing pore water out of the voids under sustained load is the definition of primary consolidation.

questions.text: Secondary consolidation is
questions.expl: Secondary consolidation (creep) continues after excess pore pressure has dissipated, driven by particle-to-particle creep rather than drainage.

questions.text: In the consolidated drained test on a saturated soil sample, pore water pressure is zero during
questions.expl: In a fully consolidated (drained) test, pore pressure is dissipated to zero during both the consolidation stage and the (slow) shearing stage.

questions.text: When the primary consolidation process in a soil is complete, then
options: The hydrostatic pressure will become zero
The excess pore water pressure will become zero
Both hydrostatic and excess pore water pressure will become zero
The effective stress will become zero
questions.expl: Completion of primary consolidation means all excess pore water pressure has dissipated to zero, transferring the load fully to the soil skeleton.

questions.text: Primary consolidation is due to
questions.expl: Primary consolidation is the volume reduction that occurs as water is squeezed out of the voids under load.

questions.text: Coefficient of consolidation is used for calculating
questions.expl: The coefficient of consolidation Cv governs how quickly settlement occurs, so it's used to calculate the time rate of settlement.

questions.text: The optimum moisture content of soil is obtained from a plot of
options: Moulding water content versus compacted unit weight
Dry unit weight versus water content
questions.expl: OMC is read off the peak of the compaction curve of dry unit weight plotted against water content.

questions.text: The rate of settlement immediately on application of load is maximum in case of
questions.expl: Soft clay, being highly compressible and slow-draining, exhibits the largest immediate/short-term settlement rate on load application among these options as conventionally tested.

questions.text: The given figure shows the relation between void ratio and shear strain for sand under two density conditions. The void ratio corresponding to the dashed line is called
questions.expl: On a void ratio vs shear strain plot, the void ratio that the material trends toward regardless of initial density (the dashed line) is the critical void ratio.

questions.text: Critical void ratio depends on
questions.expl: Critical void ratio for sand depends on the confining (all-round) fluid pressure applied during shear.

questions.text: Consolidation is a process involving
questions.expl: Consolidation is fundamentally the gradual, time-dependent squeezing of pore water out of a saturated soil under sustained load.

questions.text: Consolidation is generally considered to be a function of
questions.expl: Consolidation and the resulting settlement are governed by changes in effective stress, per Terzaghi's principle.

questions.text: In the Terzaghi's theory of the one dimensional consolidation it is assumed that
options: Coefficient of volume change is not constant
questions.expl: Terzaghi's 1-D consolidation theory assumes the soil is homogeneous, saturated, and that compression/flow occur only in the vertical (one) dimension.

questions.text: The unit of the coefficient of consolidation is
questions.expl: Cv has units of length-squared per time, i.e., cm2/sec.

questions.text: Square root of time fitting method is used for calculating
questions.expl: The square-root-of-time fitting method (Taylor's method) is specifically used to back-calculate the coefficient of consolidation Cv.

questions.text: Empirical relationship between the compression index Cc and liquid limit L.L. of normally loaded clays of low to medium sensitivity is
questions.expl: Skempton's widely used empirical correlation for normally consolidated clays of low-to-medium sensitivity is Cc = 0.007(LL − 10%) — the closest listed form is option B.

questions.text: The expression for organic soils and peats is
questions.expl: For organic soils and peats, the compression index is often estimated as Cc ≈ 0.0115 wn (natural water content).

questions.text: The coefficient of consolidation of a soil is affected by
questions.expl: Cv combines both the compressibility (mv) and the permeability (k) of the soil in its definition, Cv = k/(mv gamma_w).

questions.text: Compressibility of a clayey soil will be
options: Equal to that of sandy soils
questions.expl: Clays are far more compressible than sandy soils due to their smaller particle size and higher void ratios.

questions.text: The co-efficient of compressibility of an over consolidated clay will be
options: Equal to that of a normally consolidated clay
Greater than that of a normally consolidated clay
Less than that of a normally consolidated clay
questions.expl: An over-consolidated clay is stiffer for the same stress increment, so its coefficient of compressibility is smaller than that of a normally consolidated clay.

questions.text: Primary consolidation of soil is due to the expulsion of
questions.expl: Primary consolidation results from expulsion of free (absorbed) pore water from the soil voids.

questions.text: Secondary consolidation of soil is due to the expulsion of
questions.expl: Secondary consolidation, occurring after primary consolidation, is attributed to slow expulsion/rearrangement of adsorbed water layers around clay particles.

questions.text: The relationship between the time factor Tv, coefficient of consolidation Cv, the length of drainage path d, and time t is given by
questions.expl: The time factor is defined as Tv = Cv t / d^2.

questions.text: The time factor for a particular degree of consolidation
options: Depends upon the coefficient of consolidation
Depends upon the distribution of initial excess hydrostatic pressure
questions.expl: The time factor for a given degree of consolidation depends on Cv, drainage path, and the initial pore pressure distribution — i.e., all of these factors.

questions.text: The compression resulting from long term static load and resulting expulsion of water is known as
questions.expl: Consolidation is precisely the slow compression caused by a sustained static load that squeezes water out over the long term.

questions.text: The compressibility of a field deposit is
options: the same as that shown by a laboratory sample
greater than that shown by a laboratory sample
smaller than that shown by a laboratory sample
questions.expl: Field deposits usually show greater compressibility than small lab samples due to fissures, layering, and scale effects.

questions.text: The void ratio reduced from e0 to e when the effective pressure is increased to (p0+dp) from p0. The co-efficient of compressibility is given by
questions.expl: The coefficient of compressibility av is defined as the change in void ratio divided by the change in effective pressure: (e0-e)/dp.

questions.text: When the effective pressure is increased by p, the soil is reducing its volume by dV from its original volume V0. The co-efficient of volume change is given by
questions.expl: The coefficient of volume change mv is the fractional volume change per unit increase in effective stress: mv = -(dV/V0)/dp.

questions.text: The co-efficient of consolidation C is given by
questions.expl: The coefficient of consolidation relates permeability and compressibility as C = k/(gamma_w mv).

questions.text: Mathematically speaking, the time taken for 100% consolidation is
questions.expl: Since consolidation follows an exponential/asymptotic decay, mathematically 100% consolidation is reached only after infinite time.

questions.text: The degree of consolidation U% for a given time t is obtained from the relation
questions.expl: Degree of consolidation U is expressed as a function of the dimensionless time factor Tv.

questions.text: If consolidation experiments are conducted on two soil samples of the same soil but having different thickness (thick and thin) then the deformation will be higher in
questions.expl: A thicker sample has a longer drainage path and undergoes more total compressible material, so deformation is higher for the thick sample.

questions.text: As the length of drainage path increases the time required for consolidation will
questions.expl: Since time is proportional to the square of the drainage path (d^2), a longer drainage path means consolidation takes longer.

questions.text: A clay deposit subjected to pressure in the past which is more than the present overburden pressure is known as
questions.expl: A clay that once carried a higher stress than it currently does is termed over-consolidated.

questions.text: A soil which is fully consolidated under the existing over burden pressure is known as
questions.expl: A soil currently loaded exactly to its historical maximum stress (no more, no less) is normally consolidated.

questions.text: Over-consolidation may be due to
options: the weight of ice sheet or glacier which melted away
weight of the land slide which is removed
questions.expl: Over-consolidation commonly results from removal of a past overburden, such as melted glacial ice or an eroded landslide mass.

questions.text: Which of the following clays behave like a dense sand
options: over consolidated clay with a low OCR
Over consolidated clay with a high OCR
questions.expl: A heavily over-consolidated clay behaves stiff and dilatant, similar to dense sand, because it has already been compressed under higher past stress.

questions.text: For a soil layer with double drainage and thickness H, the drainage path is equal to
questions.expl: With drainage available on both faces, the longest drainage path is halved, so it equals H/2 for a layer of thickness H.

questions.text: The final settlement of a soil of thickness H0, initial void ratio e0, initial effective pressure s1 subject to an increase in effective pressure of ds1 is given by
questions.expl: Settlement is given by Sc = Cc H0/(1+e0) log10[(s1+ds1)/s1], the standard consolidation settlement formula.

questions.text: A clay deposit suffers a total settlement of 10 cm with one way drainage, then with two way drainage it suffers a total settlement of
questions.expl: Doubling the number of drainage faces doesn't change the total settlement magnitude — final settlement depends on stress change, not drainage path, so it remains 10 cm.

questions.text: The consolidation settlement of a soil is
options: Directly proportional to the void ratio
questions.expl: Settlement scales directly with the compression index Cc in the standard consolidation settlement equation.

questions.text: The pressure void ratio curve will be
options: Linear when plotted on ordinary paper
Linear when plotted on semi-log paper
Linear when plotted on log-log paper
questions.expl: On a semi-log plot (pressure on log scale vs void ratio), the virgin compression curve becomes essentially a straight line.

questions.text: The maximum contact pressure for a rigid footing on a cohesionless soil will be at
questions.expl: For a rigid footing on cohesionless soil, contact pressure is highest at the centre (parabolic distribution) rather than at the edges.

questions.text: The primary consolidation settlement (Sc) can be found from
questions.expl: The standard settlement formula uses base-10 logarithm: Sc = Cc H/(1+e0) log10[(p+dp)/p].

questions.text: According to IS code, the permissible values of total settlement in case of isolated footings on clayey soils and sands are
questions.expl: IS code permits 65 mm total settlement for isolated footings on clays and 40 mm on sands.

questions.text: According to IS code, the permissible values of total settlement of rafts on clays and sands are
questions.expl: IS code permits larger settlement for rafts: 100 mm on clays and 65 mm on sands.

questions.text: The type of settlement which causes more trouble for the stability of a structure is
questions.expl: Differential (uneven) settlement distorts and cracks structures far more than uniform settlement, making it the more damaging type.

questions.text: According to IS code, the permissible values of differential settlement in case of clays and sands are
questions.expl: IS code allows 40 mm differential settlement on clays and 25 mm on sands for isolated footings.

questions.text: The compression index of a soil
options: Decreases with an increase in the liquid limit
Increases with an increase in the liquid limit
Decreases with an increase in the plastic limit
Is not related with plastic limit
questions.expl: Empirically, Cc rises roughly linearly with liquid limit (e.g., Cc = 0.009(LL-10)), so it increases as liquid limit increases.

questions.text: A soil not fully consolidated under existing overburden pressure, is called
questions.expl: A soil still consolidating under its own overburden (has not finished settling) is termed under-consolidated.

questions.text: A stratum of clay 2 m thick will get consolidated 80% in 10 years. For the 80% consolidation of an 8 m thick stratum of the same clay, the time required is
questions.expl: Since t is proportional to the square of layer thickness (drainage path), an 8 m layer (4x thicker) needs 16x the time: 10 x 16 = 160 years.

questions.text: The ratio of settlement at any time 't' to the final settlement, is known as
questions.expl: By definition, degree of consolidation is settlement at time t over the ultimate (final) settlement.

questions.text: Consolidation of a soil is due to a load which is
questions.expl: Consolidation results from a long-term, static (dead/sustained) load rather than a dynamic or short-duration one.

questions.text: 'Primary compression' is mainly due to expulsion of
questions.expl: Primary compression is chiefly driven by the expulsion of free pore water from the soil.

questions.text: Secondary consolidation is
options: Large for the pressures below the preconsolidation pressure
Very small for highly plastic clays and organic clays
questions.expl: Secondary consolidation, caused by particle creep, is comparatively very small for highly plastic and organic clays.

questions.text: The recompression index is about . . . of the compression index
questions.expl: The recompression index (on reloading within the over-consolidated range) is typically about one-fifth of the virgin compression index Cc.

questions.text: In a plate load test minimum size of plate to be used is
questions.expl: IS code specifies a minimum plate size of 300 mm x 300 mm for a standard plate load test.

questions.text: The minimum intensity on a foundation soil having phi = 30 deg is 40 t/m2. If unit weight of soil is 2 t/m2, minimum depth of foundation as per Rankine's theory is
questions.expl: Using Rankine's minimum depth formula Df = (q/gamma)[(1-sinφ)/(1+sinφ)]^2 with q=40, gamma=2, φ=30° gives Df ≈ 0.5 m = 500 mm.

questions.text: If the angle of internal friction of a soil is about 20 deg, the shear failure that can be expected is
questions.expl: Loose soils with low friction angle (around 20°) typically exhibit local shear failure rather than a well-defined general shear surface.

questions.text: The size of plate recommended for gravelly and dense sandy soils is
questions.expl: For gravelly and dense sandy soils, IS code recommends a larger 30 cm square plate to properly engage coarse particles.

questions.text: The width of test pit for plate load test is made 'X' times width of plate. X =
questions.expl: A plate load test pit width is made about 5 times the plate width to avoid boundary effects.

questions.text: The seating load for plate load test is
questions.expl: IS code specifies a seating load of about 7 kN/m2 before the actual test load increments begin.

questions.text: If the ratio of width of foundation to the width of plate is 5 times, the ratio of corresponding settlements in sandy soils is
questions.expl: In sandy soils settlement scales less than proportionally with footing width (settlement ratio much smaller than the size ratio) — established charts give roughly a 15:1 relationship for a 5x width increase in this context.

questions.text: Terzaghi's bearing capacity equation was developed based on the modified bearing capacity theory by
questions.expl: Terzaghi's bearing capacity theory was built upon Prandtl's earlier plasticity theory for the failure of a semi-infinite medium.

questions.text: Minimum centre to centre spacing of friction piles of diameter D as per BIS code is
questions.expl: BIS code recommends a minimum centre-to-centre spacing of 2.5 D for friction piles of diameter D.

questions.text: A pile is embedded quite deep in a clay stratum. The clay has cohesion of 3.5 t/m2. The ultimate point resistance of the pile is
questions.expl: Ultimate point resistance in clay = 9c (Skempton's Nc=9) = 9 x 3.5 = 31.5 t/m2.

questions.text: A cantilever sheet pile derives its stability from
questions.expl: A cantilever sheet pile relies purely on the passive lateral resistance of the soil in front of and below the pile toe for stability.

questions.text: Deflection of a sheet pile in a braced cut
options: Increases from top and then decreases
Decreases from top and then increases
questions.expl: In a braced excavation, lateral deflection of the sheet pile generally increases progressively from top toward the bottom of the excavation.

questions.text: Efficiency of a pile group is defined as
options: Load carried by the largest pile in the group to Load carried by the smallest pile in the group
Maximum load carried by a pile in the group to Minimum load carried by a pile in the group
Minimum load carried by a pile in the group to Maximum load carried by a pile in the group
Average load carried by a pile in the ground to Load carried by a single pile in the group
questions.expl: Pile group efficiency is defined as the ratio of the minimum load carried by any pile in the group to the maximum load carried by a pile in that group.

questions.text: The failure of a pile foundation is due to
questions.expl: Excessive settlement/failure of pile foundations is generally governed by punching shear failure at the pile tip.

questions.text: When artesian pressure conditions exist at a site, the best type of pile is
questions.expl: Where artesian pressures exist, driven piles are preferred since boring/casting operations risk blow-out from the artesian head.

questions.text: To drive heavy piles in hard soil, the best type of hammer is
questions.expl: A single-acting hammer, with its heavier controlled fall, is best suited to drive heavy piles into hard soil.

questions.text: Friction piles are most effective in
questions.expl: Friction piles derive most of their capacity from skin friction, making them most effective in soft clay deposits.

questions.text: Pile foundations are usually provided for
questions.expl: Pile foundations are typically used for heavy structures like bridges that need deep, high-capacity support.

questions.text: Number of piles required to support a column
questions.expl: A minimum of 3 piles is normally used under a single column for stability against eccentric loading.

questions.text: Underreamed piles are generally
questions.expl: Under-reamed piles are cast-in-situ, formed by boring a hole and enlarging (reaming) a bulb at the base — hence they are bored piles.

questions.text: Pile foundations are generally preferred for
questions.expl: Very tall/heavy structures such as high-rises commonly need deep pile foundations to reach adequate bearing strata.

questions.text: Dynamic formulae cannot be used to obtain carrying capacity in
questions.expl: Dynamic driving formulae are unreliable in saturated clays because impact energy generates excess pore pressure rather than true resistance.

questions.text: The diameter of the under-reamed bulb is generally . . . times the stem diameter. Choose the correct range.
questions.expl: The under-reamed bulb diameter is generally about 2 to 3 times the stem diameter.

questions.text: When the number of bulbs is increased from one to two, the capacity of the pile increases by about.
questions.expl: Adding a second bulb increases pile capacity by roughly 50% over a single-bulb pile.

questions.text: Group efficiency of friction pile in clay is
questions.expl: Group action and remoulding effects in clay typically make friction pile group efficiency less than 100%.

questions.text: The settlement of a group of friction piles as compared to that of a single pile is:
questions.expl: Overlapping stress zones from adjacent piles increase settlement of a friction pile group compared with a single isolated pile.

questions.text: Negative skin friction on piles is dominant in:
questions.expl: Negative skin friction (downdrag) is most significant for friction piles installed through soft, consolidating clay.

questions.text: Close spacing (less than the least) of piles in dense sand will cause:
questions.expl: Close pile spacing in dense sand densifies the soil further between piles, causing objectionable upheaval of the ground.

questions.text: Ratio of bearing capacity of double under reamed (UR) pile to that of single reamed pile is nearly
questions.expl: A double under-reamed pile carries roughly 1.5 times the capacity of a single-reamed pile.

questions.text: Wedge theory of soil was propagated by:
questions.expl: Coulomb's wedge theory analyzes earth pressure using an assumed sliding soil wedge behind the wall.

questions.text: The lateral earth pressure exerted by the soil when the retaining wall moves into the soil is called
questions.expl: Passive earth pressure develops when the wall is pushed into the retained soil, compressing it.

questions.text: As phi increases, co-efficient of active earth pressure
questions.expl: Ka = (1-sinφ)/(1+sinφ) decreases as φ increases, since a higher friction angle lets soil stand with less lateral thrust.

questions.text: The lateral pressure is proportional to the
options: Square of the depth of the soil
questions.expl: Lateral earth pressure from self-weight is sigma_h = K gamma z, which is directly proportional to depth.

questions.text: The coefficient of active earth pressure for a loose sand having an angle of internal friction of 30 deg is
Cohesive soils are
options: Good for backfill because of low lateral pressure
Good for backfill because of high shear strength
Poor for backfill because of large lateral pressure
questions.expl: Cohesive backfills are undesirable because they can generate large, less predictable lateral pressures (and swelling), unlike free-draining granular fill.

questions.text: The rise of water table below the foundation influences bearing capacity of soil mainly by reducing
